paragraphs: It can be seen from the last chapter that the way general business is managed gives a fairly clear indication of the actual state of morals and the health of the body politic. The more harmony reigns in the assemblies, that is, the closer opinion comes to unanimity, the more dominant the general will is. On the other hand, long debates, dissensions and tumult announce the rise of particular interests and the decline of the State.

This seems less clear when two or more orders enter into the constitution, as the patricians and plebeians did at Rome. Quarrels between these two orders often disturbed the comitia, even in the best days of the Republic. But the exception is more apparent than real. Because of a defect inherent in the body politic, there were then, so to speak, two States in one, and what is not true of the two together is true of each separately. Indeed, even in the stormiest times, the plebiscita of the people, when the Senate did not interfere with them, always went through quietly and by large majorities. The citizens having only one interest, the people had a single will.

At the other extreme of the circle, unanimity returns. This happens when the citizens, having fallen into servitude, have lost both liberty and will. Fear and flattery then turn votes into acclamation. Deliberation ceases, and only worship or cursing is left. Such was the vile way the Senate expressed its views under the Emperors. It sometimes did so with absurd precautions. Tacitus observes that under Otho the senators, while heaping curses on Vitellius, managed at the same time to make a deafening noise, so that if he ever became their master he would not know what each of them had said.

On these various considerations depend the rules for counting votes and comparing opinions. These rules should be set according to how easy or hard the general will is to discover, and how far the State has declined.

There is only one law that by its nature requires unanimous consent. This is the social compact, for civil association is the most voluntary of all acts. Every man is born free and his own master, so no one, under any pretext whatever, can make any man a subject without his consent. To decide that the son of a slave is born a slave is to decide that he is not born a man.

If, then, there are opponents when the social compact is made, their opposition does not invalidate the contract. It merely keeps them from being included in it. They are foreigners among citizens. Once the State is instituted, residence constitutes consent. To live within its territory is to submit to the Sovereign.[1]

Apart from this original contract, the vote of the majority always binds all the rest. This follows from the contract itself. But it is asked how a man can be both free and forced to conform to wills that are not his own. How can the opponents be both free and subject to laws they have not agreed to?

I reply that the question is wrongly put. The citizen consents to all the laws, including those passed in spite of his opposition, and even those that punish him when he dares to break any of them. The constant will of all the members of the State is the general will, and by it they are citizens and free.[2] When a law is proposed in the popular assembly, what the people is asked is not exactly whether it approves or rejects the proposal, but whether it conforms to the general will, which is their will. Each man, in giving his vote, states his opinion on that point, and the general will is found by counting the votes. When, therefore, the opinion contrary to mine prevails, this proves neither more nor less than that I was mistaken, and that what I thought to be the general will was not. If my particular opinion had carried the day, I would have achieved the opposite of what I willed, and in that case I would not have been free.
This presupposes, indeed, that all the qualities of the general will still reside in the majority. When they cease to do so, then whatever side a man takes, liberty is no longer possible.

In my earlier demonstration of how particular wills are substituted for the general will in public deliberation, I pointed out adequately the practical ways of avoiding this abuse, and I shall have more to say of them later. I have also given the principles for determining the proportion of votes needed to declare that will. A difference of one vote destroys equality, and a single opponent destroys unanimity. But between equality and unanimity there are several degrees of unequal division, and at any of them this proportion may be fixed, according to the condition and needs of the body politic.

Two general rules may serve to regulate this relation. First, the graver and more important the questions discussed, the closer to unanimity the prevailing opinion should be. Second, the more the matter in hand calls for speed, the smaller the required difference in votes may be allowed to become. Where an immediate decision has to be reached, a majority of one vote should be enough. The first of these two rules seems more in harmony with the laws, and the second with practical affairs. In any case, it is the combination of the two that gives the best proportions for determining the necessary majority.
